title: What is three.js TSL, and why use it?
transcript: Hello everyone, I'm Shiaa. If you've written custom shaders in 3.js, you're probably familiar with before compile hacks or writing GLSL strings by hand. These methods work, but they often lead to code that's difficult to maintain and reuse. Today, let's talk about the official solution from 3.js, TSL, which brings us a more modern engineering focused shader workflow. First, TSL 3.js JS shading language is essentially a shader construction system and abstraction layer. Look at this diagram dot we work on the far left writing logic in familiar JavaScript or TypeScript. The TSL engine in the middle acts as a compiler gesture sweeps to the right. It builds our highle code into the low-level shader language required by the target platform GLSL for WebGL or WGSL for web GPU. This process is fully automatic. The immediate benefit of this abstraction is improved code readability and maintainability. This image compares the two approaches. On the right is the traditional shader material method where GLSL code exists as strings, lacks type checking and is disconnected from the JavaScript logic. On the left is the TSL approach which is declarative and nodebased. Every operation is a reusable function or node, making the logic clear and structured. This not only reduces the chance of errors, but also makes code reuse and refactoring significantly easier. In short, TSL transforms shader code from imagic strings into the modular code we manage and maintain daily. Besides improving the developer experience, TSL also solves several key engineering problems. First, cross-platform compatibility. Webqu is the future, but we can't abandon WebGL support just yet. TSL smooths over the syntactical differences between GLSL and WGSL. A single set of node logic you write can run seamlessly on both rendering pipelines. This significantly reduces the cost of project migration and maintenance. Second, non-destructively extending existing materials. In the past, if you wanted to add a special effect to a standard mesh standard material, like the subsurface scattering lighting model in lists flame lotus, you'd likely have to copy and modify large chunks of 3.js's internal GLSL code. This is tedious and prone to breaking with version updates. TSL, however, let you use mesh standard node material to programmatically replace or extend a specific part of the material, like its color, color node, or normal normal node. you can preserve the powerful lighting calculations of the PBR material and only inject the custom logic you need. This is a much more stable and modular way to extend materials. Third, leveraging the GPU for general purpose computing. The complex fluid simulation shown in this image is driven by intensive mathematical calculations. TSL combined with WebGPU's compute shaders provides a JavaScript API for executing generalpurpose parallel computations on the GPU. This means we can offload data inensive tasks like physics simulations for particle systems or complex algorithms and data visualization from the CPU to the GPU. This frees up the main thread and dramatically improves application performance. TSL provides a structured entry point for these kinds of computational tasks. So to summarize, TSL isn't just for creating visual effects. It's an engineering solution that improves the shader development workflow, code quality, and application performance. It provides code modularity, platform compatibility, material extensibility, and access to generalpurpose GPU computing.
